analysis.one_liner: Exempts most replacement parts for existing equipment from new federal chemical restrictions.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee with one cosponsor on January 21, 2026; no hearing, vote, or further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: When the Environmental Protection Agency restricts a chemical under the Toxic Substances Control Act, it can effectively ban that chemical in products — including the parts needed to repair equipment people already own. This bill requires EPA to keep replacement parts for complex durable goods and complex consumer goods that were designed before a restriction was issued available, unless the agency can prove with substantial evidence that the part by itself significantly adds to public health risk. Any restriction that does apply to parts would allow at least a 10-year transition, and the chemicals needed to make exempt parts could not be banned upstream.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of existing equipment — heating and cooling systems, vehicles, appliances — who would keep being able to buy repair parts instead of replacing expensive machines early, and the manufacturers and importers of those parts, who could keep making them with chemicals even after EPA restricts those chemicals elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Repair shops, parts makers, equipment owners

how_it_helps.text: EPA must exempt replacement parts for complex durable goods and complex consumer goods designed before a restriction rule is published, so repair parts for equipment people already own stay legal to make and import.

EPA may only regulate such a part if it makes a written determination, backed by substantial evidence in the risk evaluation, that the part by itself significantly contributes to risk — a deliberately high bar that keeps parts from being swept into bans aimed at other products.
Any restriction that does reach replacement parts must allow a transition period of at least 10 years, giving manufacturers and repair networks time to retool.
Chemicals needed to make exempt parts cannot be prohibited at the manufacturing, processing, or import stage, with procedures limiting that production to replacement-parts makers.

analysis.who_pays: The general public bears any continued exposure to chemicals used in exempt parts, even chemicals EPA has restricted in other products, for at least a decade under any new rule; EPA's authority to protect health through product rules is also narrowed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through continued chemical exposure

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a chemical that EPA has restricted in new products keep flowing into the parts supply for existing equipment for at least 10 years, extending exposure that a risk evaluation identified.

The exception standard requires EPA to prove the replacement part alone — not the equipment it belongs to — significantly contributes to risk, supported by substantial evidence; because a single part usually contributes only a fraction of a product's risk, this makes regulation of parts practically very difficult.
Once replacement parts are excluded from a risk evaluation, the rule itself becomes final agency action on that exclusion, limiting future challenges to keeping those parts exempt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real consumer benefit: if the chemicals in repair parts are banned without a carve-out, expensive equipment like heating systems and vehicles can become unrepairable and people are forced to replace them early. But the bill goes further than a narrow repairability fix — it sets a proof standard that makes parts nearly impossible to regulate and guarantees at least 10 more years of production for any restricted chemical used in them. An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: repairability today in exchange for continued chemical exposure under rules that would otherwise phase it out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat without any hearing or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Hudson introduced the bill in the House on January 21, 2026, together with Rep. Balderson.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only action taken on it so far.
The bill has one cosponsor and has received no hearing, markup, or floor vote in the record to date.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete: current chemical rules still apply, and the parts industry has lost nothing while the bill sits in committee. If it stays there, the status quo — EPA free to restrict chemicals in replacement parts under existing law — continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill just sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Richard Hudson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the Toxic Substances Control Act's replacement-parts exemption and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Troy Balderson
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans are on the record — the sponsor and his sole cosponsor — and no votes or hearings have occurred, so the partisan shape is not yet visible.

industries.note: The bill guarantees they can keep making and importing parts with restricted chemicals for equipment designed before a rule, and bars upstream bans on the chemicals those parts need. Consumers share the benefit when it keeps their equipment repairable, but share the cost of continued chemical exposure.

industries.industry: Equipment and appliance makers with large installed bases
industries.note: Companies that sold heating systems, vehicles, and appliances containing soon-to-be-restricted chemicals keep a legal parts stream, protecting customers from forced replacement and protecting the makers from warranty and service disruption. It also prolongs the use of the chemicals those products contain.

Even after EPA restricts a chemical substance in products, the bill keeps demand alive by barring prohibition of the chemical's manufacture, processing, or import when it is destined for exempt replacement parts. The public bears the continued exposure that the restriction was meant to end.

industries.industry: EPA's regulatory authority over chemicals in commerce
industries.note: The agency's power to restrict chemicals in replacement parts is cut back to a narrow exception requiring a substantial-evidence finding that the part alone drives risk, plus a 10-year transition in any case.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with one cosponsor referred to Energy and Commerce rarely reaches the floor on its own in the remainder of a two-year Congress. More likely paths are stalling in committee or surfacing as an amendment to a larger bill moving chemical or manufacturing policy, since replacement-parts exemptions have come up in debates over EPA chemical rules.
